turns: The year is 1930. The helium nucleus has a mass of four units but a charge of only two. How do physicists account for this difference?
answers: The discrepancy between the charge and the mass of the helium nucleus is explained on the assumption that the charge is concentrated at the centre of the nucleus, while the matter composing the nucleus is distributed uniformly round the charge. In other words, the charge is regarded as positive, and the matter negative electricity. The positive charge produces a repulsion between itself and the negative matter, which causes the latter to assume a spherical form. The positive charge in the centre is balanced by an equal and opposite charge on the surface, and the excess of matter over charge constitutes the nucleus. The charge on the surface is equal to twice the charge in the centre, and the total charge on the nucleus is therefore four units. The matter composing the nucleus occupies a volume equal to one-fourth of the volume of the sphere, and has therefore a volume-density of one unit. The negative matter of the nucleus has, accordingly, the same volume-density as the positive charge, and consequently the nucleus has a uniform density throughout. The unit volume-density of negative matter is called the specific negative gravity of the nucleus. Bekker, in 1846, suggested a similar explanation of the discrepancy between charge and mass in the case of the hydrogen atom. (See Thomson and Tait’s ‘Natural Philosophy,’ Part I., § 258).

The positive charge was regarded as being concentrated at a single point, and the negative charges were spread over a sphere with the positive point as centre, so that the total charge was uniform. turns: What did Sir Ernest Rutherford suggest in his Bakerian Lecture of 1920 concerning the constitution of atomic nuclei?
answers: Sir Ernest Rutherford suggested in his Bakerian Lecture of 1920 that the nuclei of atoms are built up of protons and electrons, the protons being positive charges of electricity, and the electrons negative charges. The number of protons in an atom is equal to the atomic weight, and the number of electrons is equal to half the atomic weight. The protons and electrons are arranged in a kind of open chain, the positive and negative charges being alternately linked together. The atom therefore consists of a positively charged central nucleus, surrounded by a number of negative electrons, the total negative charge being equal to the positive charge. The remaining space is filled with ether. (See _Atom_, and _Electron_.)

turns: What is the story of Mr. H. G. Wells's novel 'The World Set Free'?
answers: Mr. H. G. Wells's novel, 'The World Set Free,' was published in 1914, and was intended to represent the probable state of affairs in Europe fifty years hence. At that time, war had been abolished, and the nations of the Continent had formed themselves into a single great federation, under the presidency of France. The immediate cause of the federation had been the realization of a great European calamity--the destruction of San Francisco by earthquake and fire in 1960. The shock of that disaster had been felt throughout the civilized world, and had shaken Europe out of its parochialisms into a fellowship of sympathies and interests. The story opens with a picture of Europe quaking and trembling in the throes of the great calamity, and closes with a prospect of its permanent pacification. The intermediate chapters describe the gradual evolution of the European States into an harmonious whole, the disappearance of national jealousies, and the establishment of a 'United Nations' parliament, which sits permanently at Paris, and controls a common European policy. The book, in fact, is an allegorical history of European progress, from chaos to cosmos, during the second half of the twentieth century. The machinery of the narrative consists partly of personal anecdote, partly of direct historical narrative, and partly of dramatic dialogue. The personal anecdotes relate chiefly to the careers of certain eminent men, who have prominent parts to play in the development of European unity--Loubet, Clemenceau, and Delcassé, among Frenchmen; Bismarck and Moltke, among Germans; and King Edward VII., among Englishmen. The historical portions of the book deal with the formation of the United Nations, the abolition of war, and the establishment of universal and compulsory arbitration. The dramatic dialogues set forth the origin and evolution of European socialism, and forecast a time when private property shall have been everywhere abolished, and the entire continent shall be managed on socialistic principles, for the equal benefit of all its inhabitants. The scheme of the book, as a whole, may be summed up in the motto borrowed from Virgil:--Eventusque probat. The final chapter leaves Europe at peace within itself, and at peace, also, with America and Asia.

answers: It means that the spiral nebulae are remote universes, and that the further they are removed from us the more rapidly are they travelling. The rate of recession at which these objects are flying through space can only be guessed at; but it must be enormous. In the case of one nebula, indeed, the rate has been estimated at not less than 400 miles a second. The bearing of this upon current theories of the stellar system is obvious. If the spiral nebulae are remote sidereal universes, then our own sidereal system must be but a component of a larger system still, and so on, in an infinite series.

turns: The year is 1930. Of what chemical substance are the genes, the units of heredity, most probably composed?
answers: The genes are very probably composed of organic matter of the nature of protein. They are probably small particles of living matter. The proof of this consists in the fact that they can be made to multiply, and that they can be killed. If a living organism be inoculated with the genes of a particular species, these multiply, and the resulting progeny also contains them. On the other hand, if the genes be killed, the resulting organisms are rendered incapable of further propagation. The particles must therefore be of vital, though minute, dimensions. Furthermore, the genes can be made to dye, and can be stained by special methods of treatment. The evidence, accordingly, points to the conclusion that they are living and organic, but small enough to elude direct observation under the highest powers of the microscope. The chemical nature of the protein of which they are composed can only be surmised. It must be of a simple kind, since the genes are inherited independently of sex, and since they can be passed on from generation to generation, apart from any conjunction of male and female reproductive elements. (Thomson, _Heredity_.)

turns: The year is 1930. Is there any truth in Professor Wegener's theory that the continents drift slowly across the face of the globe?
answers: There is no truth in the theory that the continents drift slowly across the face of the globe. The earth has a motion of rotation on its own axis, from west to east, and the continents partake of this motion. The apparent movement from east to west is due to the fact that the spectator himself moves from west to east. The earth turns from west to east at the rate of about 1,000 miles an hour, which is equal to 16·7 miles a minute. The motion is uniform, and the continents keep pace with it. In 24 hours they drift 360 degrees, and in a year they complete the circuit of the globe. If Europe be taken as the starting-point, in twelve months it will have passed under Africa, Asia, and America, and come back to Europe again. During the process, each continental region has been successively subjected to all meridians, from 0 to 180, east and west. The shifting scenes of a panorama are not more real than the apparent motion of the lands. The fact is obvious enough, but the explanation of it involves some difficult questions of physical science, which cannot be discussed here.
